books.section: Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: National Interstate and Defense Highways Act, 1956

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); images are public-domain photographs viewed before writing

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the federal government shaped the American economy between 1945 and 1980.

documents.title: The GI Bill
documents.source: Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A federal law for returning veterans, written to move millions of soldiers into civilian life.
documents.text: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act offered returning veterans low-interest loans to buy homes and money to attend college. By 1956, nearly eight million veterans had used its education benefits, and by 1955 the Veterans Administration had backed more than 4.3 million home loans. The benefits reached African American veterans unevenly, since states set the rules for extending them.

documents.title: The Taft-Hartley Act
documents.source: Taft-Hartley Act, 1947, passed over President Truman's veto. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A law passed by a conservative Congress elected in 1946, written to restrict organized labor after the strike wave.
documents.text: The Taft-Hartley Act limited unions' ability to strike, let states pass right-to-work laws banning union shops, and required union leaders to swear they were not Communists. Labor unions called the act a slave-labor law. The act showed the government moving from the union backing of the 1930s toward restriction of labor.

documents.title: The Marshall Plan
documents.source: Account of the Marshall Plan, 1948-1951. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A summary of the American aid program for Europe, written from the government's stated goals and results.
documents.text: The Marshall Plan sent American aid to rebuild war-torn Europe. Seventeen nations received aid between 1948 and 1951, with West Germany, France, and Britain receiving the bulk of it. The plan stabilized the capitalist economies of Western Europe and raised living standards there, offering a working alternative to Soviet-style Communism.

documents.title: The Interstate Highway Act
documents.source: National Interstate and Defense Highways Act, 1956. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A federal law sold as a defense measure, written when the government was building the postwar highway system.
documents.text: The National Interstate and Defense Highways Act launched a massive federal highway-building project. The highways were promoted as a defense measure, to move troops and military equipment quickly, and they let drivers travel fast from suburbs into cities. The roads made it easy to live in a suburb and drive to work in a city.

documents.title: Poverty amid affluence
documents.source: Michael Harrington, The Other America (1962). Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: A writer and socialist activist describing poverty the postwar boom had not removed, written to push the government to act.
documents.text: Forty to fifty million Americans lived in poverty, many in decaying urban slums and many in isolated rural towns. Machines and automation, which raised output for the nation, took jobs from farm workers and factory workers and left them poor. The book helped shape the domestic agendas of Presidents Kennedy and Johnson.

documents.title: The WIN button
documents.source: A red and white WIN button from President Gerald R. Ford's 1974 Whip Inflation Now campaign. Public domain (U.S. government), via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: A campaign button handed out by the Ford administration, showing how the government asked the public to fight inflation.
documents.text: The photograph shows a round red button with the white letters WIN. President Gerald Ford's administration gave out the buttons in 1974 as part of the Whip Inflation Now campaign, which asked Americans to cut unnecessary spending and consumption.

documents.title: Odd and even days at the pump
documents.source: Photograph: gasoline station in Oregon, fall 1973. EPA DOCUMERICA photograph (NARA 555489), public domain (U.S. government photograph), via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: An EPA photograph of the gasoline crisis, showing how the shortage reached ordinary drivers.
documents.text: The photograph shows a gasoline station in Oregon in the fall of 1973. A black sign reads EVEN NUMBERS ONLY, and cars wait in line at the pumps. A sign on one car reads LAST CAR OUT OF GAS.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the federal government shaped the American economy between 1945 and 1980, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of the government's shaping does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the wartime economy, the New Deal's expansion of federal power, or the Cold War.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant content from at least three documents, such as the GI Bill, the Taft-Hartley Act, or the Marshall Plan.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument about the government's economic role.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the baby boom, Levittown, the Sunbelt migration, or the Department of Energy.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement about the government with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation for at least two documents, such as Harrington's purpose in exposing poverty or Ford's purpose in handing out WIN buttons.
rubric.notEarned: Describing what a document says without explaining why its source matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the thesis by period, explaining why the government's role grew and then faltered, or weighing the government's power against the limits shown in the 1970s.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The federal government shaped the postwar economy deeply, building suburbs, highways, and a global trading order through its spending and laws, though its power over the economy weakened in the 1970s when oil prices and stagflation escaped its control.
Context: The wartime economy had put the federal government at the center of production, and the New Deal had already made Washington a major economic actor before the war.
Evidence: Documents 1, 3, and 4 show the government building the postwar boom, through GI Bill loans, Marshall Plan aid, and the highway system. Document 2 shows the government restricting labor through Taft-Hartley. Documents 5, 6, and 7 show the limits: poverty that growth did not remove, a WIN campaign that asked instead of ordered, and gas lines the government could not fill.
Outside evidence: Levittown and the Sunbelt migration show federal loans and highways reshaping where Americans lived, and the baby boom drove demand for houses and schools.
Complexity: The government's shaping was real but changed over time. In the 1950s its spending built prosperity, while in the 1970s its tools failed against foreign oil and rising prices, so the extent of its power shrank even as its spending stayed large.
